title: Best Dehumidifier for Plants (2026) & Using Its Water on Them
h1: The Best Dehumidifiers for Plants (and Can You Use the Water on Them?)
dek: Most houseplants want more humidity, not less. Here's how to tell when a plant room really is too damp — and what to do with all that collected water.
description: When plants really need a dehumidifier, the best picks for plant rooms and shelves, and whether dehumidifier water for plants is safe to use on houseplants.
intro: Two questions bring most people here: does my plant room need a dehumidifier, and can I use **dehumidifier water for plants**? The short answers are "probably not" and "usually, with care." Most common houseplants are happiest at **40–60%** relative humidity, and tropical varieties often prefer **60–80%** — higher than many homes manage in winter with the heat running. For a typical collection, a humidifier helps more than a dehumidifier.

There is one situation where drier air is the right fix: a room crowded with plants, misted often or sitting on pebble trays, that stays humid enough to invite powdery mildew, gray mold, fungus gnats or root rot. That's the job the units below are chosen for — and we start with the tool that tells you whether you're in that situation at all.
topPicksLead: Before buying any dehumidifier, start with the **AcuRite 01080M Pro hygrometer** to confirm your plant room really runs too humid; if it does, the **Midea Cube 20** is our pick for a sunroom or plant room.

blocks.text: The gap between the first two numbers is why "too dry" is a far more common houseplant problem than "too humid." Damp-air trouble tends to be local: tightly grouped foliage with little airflow can create a pocket far more humid than the wall-mounted reading suggests.

sections.heading: How we pick dehumidifiers for plants

blocks.text: We don't grow test plants or run a lab. We started from university extension guidance (Penn State and UC IPM) on houseplant humidity and disease, then matched products to the specific spaces where excess humidity actually occurs: enclosed shelves, sunrooms and dedicated plant rooms.

For each pick we compared published capacity and coverage, whether the humidistat can hold a moderate target rather than just running flat-out, noise for rooms people use, and owner reports. A diagnostic hygrometer comes first because it decides whether you need anything else.

sections.heading: What to look for in a dehumidifier for plants

items.label: Proof you need one
items.text: A week of hygrometer readings above 60–70% near your plants. Below 40%, you need a humidifier instead — see [dehumidifier vs. humidifier](/guides/dehumidifier-vs-humidifier/).

items.label: A settable humidistat
items.text: Plants want moderate humidity. Choose a unit that stops at a target like 55–60% instead of running continuously.

items.label: The right scale
items.text: A silica canister for a shelf or closet; a compressor unit for a full room.

items.label: Airflow, too
items.text: A small fan between plant groupings reduces mildew risk regardless of the room's overall humidity.

sections.heading: Signs your plant room is too humid

items: A powdery white coating on leaves (powdery mildew).
Fuzzy gray mold on stems, flowers or the soil surface.
Clouds of tiny fungus gnats when you water.
Potting mix that stays wet for a week or more after watering.
Condensation running down windows most mornings.

blocks.title: Fix the watering first
blocks.text: Root rot is driven mainly by waterlogged potting mix. A humid room slows drying, but cutting back on watering often solves more than any dehumidifier will on its own.

sections.heading: Can you use dehumidifier water for plants?

blocks.text: Generally, yes — for ornamental houseplants. The water in your dehumidifier's tank is condensed from the air, so it starts out very low in dissolved minerals, a bit like distilled water. That makes it appealing for plants that dislike hard tap water. But it isn't sterile or purified, so use it with a few precautions.

items: **Use it fresh.** Water that sits in a warm tank for days can grow bacteria and mold. Empty and use it within a day or so.
**Keep the tank clean.** Rinse and wipe the bucket regularly so you're not pouring biofilm onto your plants.
**Stick to ornamentals.** Condensate can pick up trace metals or dust from the coils and tank, so most advice is to skip it for edible plants and herbs.
**Don't drink it.** It isn't safe for people or pets — see [can you drink dehumidifier water?](/guides/can-you-drink-dehumidifier-water/).

blocks.text: Not in any meaningful way. Some plants are often promoted as natural dehumidifiers because their leaves can take up a little moisture, but overall, plants release water vapor through transpiration — that's why a crowded plant room gets humid in the first place. If a room is genuinely damp, plants won't fix it; ventilation and a dehumidifier will. For other approaches, read [how to dehumidify a room](/guides/how-to-dehumidify-a-room/).

Most houseplants want more humidity than a typical home provides, so start with the **AcuRite 01080M Pro** hygrometer before buying anything. If your plant room really does run humid, the **Eva-Dry E-333** handles a shelf or closet, the **Midea Cube 20** holds a sunroom at a plant-friendly target, and the **Pro Breeze 30-Pint** steps up for a large collection. And yes, fresh dehumidifier water from a clean tank is fine for ornamental plants — just not for edibles or for drinking.

faqs.q: Can you use dehumidifier water for plants?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, for ornamental houseplants. It's low in minerals, but it isn't purified, so use it fresh from a clean tank and avoid using it on edible plants and herbs.

faqs.q: Is dehumidifier water good for plants?
faqs.a: It can be helpful for plants that are sensitive to hard tap water, because condensate contains very few dissolved minerals. The main risks are bacteria from a dirty or stagnant tank and trace contaminants from the unit itself.

Usually not. Most houseplants prefer 40–60% humidity and tropicals often like more, while many homes run drier than that in winter. A dehumidifier helps only when a crowded plant room stays consistently humid enough to cause mildew, mold or gnats.
None do so meaningfully. Plants release moisture through transpiration, so a room full of them typically gets more humid, not less.

faqs.q: Should I get a humidifier or a dehumidifier for my plants?
faqs.a: Check a hygrometer first. Below about 40%, most houseplants benefit from a humidifier. If a plant-filled room stays above 60–70% with condensation or mildew, a dehumidifier is the right tool.

faqs.q: What humidity causes powdery mildew on houseplants?
faqs.a: High humidity combined with poor airflow is the trigger. UC IPM advises keeping indoor plant spaces below 85% to discourage fungal disease, and a fan between dense plant groupings helps a lot.
